rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is Medinan, revealed at different times; Ibn ʿAṭiyya identifies the verse warning of return to God as the last revelation to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مدنية، نزلت في مدد شتى، وفيها آخر آية نزلت على رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، وهي:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baqara is called the Qurʾān’s tent because of its stature and beauty and the legal rulings and exhortations it contains.
rows.anchor: ويقال لسورة البقرة: «فسطاط القرآن» وذلك لعظمها وبهائها وما تضمنت من الأحكام والمواعظ

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar learned the surah’s jurisprudence and all its sciences over eight years.
rows.anchor: وتعلمها عبد الله بن عمر رضي الله عنهما بفقهها وجميع ما تحتوي عليه من العلوم في ثمانية أعوام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is said to contain five hundred rulings and fifteen parables.
rows.anchor: وفيها خمسمائة حكم، وخمسة عشر مثلا

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In a report transmitted by al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan, the Prophet names al-Baqara the best surah and Ayat al-Kursī the best verse.
rows.anchor: وروى الحسن بن أبي الحسن أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: «أي القرآن أفضل؟»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is said that the meanings of its verses of mercy, hope, and punishment reach three hundred and sixty.
rows.anchor: ويقال إن آيات الرحمة والرجاء والعذاب تنتهي فيها معانيها إلى ثلاثمائة وستين معنى

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet was given al-Baqara from the earlier scripture, Ṭā Hā and the Ṭawāsīn from Moses’s tablets, and al-Fātiḥa and the surah’s closing verses from beneath the Throne.
rows.anchor: أعطيت سورة البقرة من الذكر الأول، وأعطيت طه والطواسين من ألواح موسى

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: An authentic hadith says al-Baqara and Āl ʿImrān will come at resurrection as paired canopies or clouds, or rows of birds, defending their reciter.
rows.anchor: في الحديث الصحيح عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال: «تجيء البقرة وآل عمران يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Al-Bukhārī transmits that reciting the final two verses of al-Baqara at night suffices the reader.
rows.anchor: وفي البخاري أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام قال: «من قرأ بالآيتين من آخر سورة البقرة في ليلة كفتاه»

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that Satan does not enter a house where al-Baqara is recited.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو هريرة عنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال: «البيت الذي تقرأ فيه سورة البقرة لا يدخله الشيطان»

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report calls al-Baqara the Qurʾān’s summit and Ayat al-Kursī its foremost verse, just as every thing has a summit.
rows.anchor: لكل شيء سنام وسنام القرآن سورة البقرة، فيها آية هي سيدة أي القرآن هي آية الكرسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives the surah’s verse count as 285, while reporting alternatives of 286 and 287.
rows.anchor: وعدد آي سورة البقرة مائتان وخمس وثمانون آية، وقيل: ست وثمانون، وقيل سبع وثمانون

rows.speaker: معمر بن المثنى
rows.claim: Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā says the particle idh is redundant, yielding the sense “and your Lord said.”
rows.anchor: إذ زائدة، والتقدير وقال ربك

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj calls Abū ʿUbayda’s claim that idh is redundant an audacious interpretation; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says all exegetes rejected it.
rows.anchor: هذا اجتراء من أبي عبيدة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority reject redundancy and connect idh to an implied command: “remember when your Lord said.”
rows.anchor: ليست بزائدة وإنما هي معلقة بفعل مقدر تقديره واذكر إذ قال

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: They also relate the passage to the prior statement that God created everything on earth for humanity, with creation beginning when He addressed the angels.
rows.anchor: خلق لكم ما في الأرض جميعا الآية، يقتضي أن يكون التقدير وابتداء خلقكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s possessive address to Muḥammad, “your Lord,” and the second-person suffix honor him and display special favor toward him.
rows.anchor: إضافة رب إلى محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم ومخاطبته بالكاف تشريف منه له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular malak is derived from malāk on the pattern mafʿal, from lāka, “to send”; malāʾika is its plural on the pattern mafāʿila.
rows.anchor: والملائكة واحدها ملك أصله ملاك على وزن مفعل من لاك إذا أرسل

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Another etymology derives malak from maʾlak, from alaka, “to send,” and parses malāʾika as its plural.
rows.anchor: أصل ملك مألك، من ألك إذا أرسل

rows.speaker: عدي بن زيد
rows.claim: The poet ʿAdī ibn Zayd uses maʾlakan as evidence for the alternative derivation of malak.
rows.anchor: أبلغ النعمان عني مألكا ... أنه قد طال حبسي وانتظاري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both laʾaka and alaka are attested; the hamza shifts after the lām, producing the form maʿfal and plural maʿāfila.
rows.anchor: اللغتان مسموعتان لأك وألك، قلبت فيه الهمزة بعد اللام فجاء وزنه معفل

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysān derives malak from malaka, treating the hamza as extra as in shamʾal from shamal, and gives the plural pattern faʿāʾila.
rows.anchor: هو من ملك يملك، والهمزة فيه زائدة كما زيدت في شمأل من شمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line preserves the word malʾak in its original form, supporting the underlying hamza analysis.
rows.anchor: فلست لأنسي ولكن لملأك ... تنزل من جو السماء يصوب

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: In ordinary speech the hamza is eased and its vowel transferred to the lām or ʿayn; the tāʾ in malāʾika marks a nonliteral feminine plural or intensification, with the first account clearer to Ibn ʿAṭiyya.
rows.anchor: والهاء في ملائكة لتأنيث الجموع غير حقيقي، وقيل هي للمبالغة كعلامة ونسابة، والأول أبين

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says the hamza in malāʾika is inserted because its singular is malak.
rows.anchor: الهمزة في ملائكة مجتلبة لأن واحدها ملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Abū ʿUbayda’s explanation is the direction toward which Ibn Kaysān inclined.
rows.anchor: فهذا الذي نحا إليه ابن كيسان

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and others explain “we sanctify You” as magnifying God and declaring His remembrance free of anything unworthy.
rows.anchor: ونقدس لك معناه ونقدسك أي نعظمك ونطهر ذكرك عما لا يليق به. قاله مجاهد وأبو صالح وغيرهما

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some interpret “we sanctify You” as “we pray to You”; Ibn ʿAṭiyya judges this weak.
rows.anchor: نقدس لك معناه نصلي لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For “I know what you do not know,” the more apparent parsing makes aʿlam a future verb and mā its direct object.
rows.anchor: الأظهر أن أعلم فعل مستقبل، وما في موضع نصب به

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: An alternative parses aʿlam as a noun with mā in the genitive as its complement.
rows.anchor: وقيل أعلم اسم، وما في موضع خفض بالإضافة

rows.speaker: سيبويه والخليل
rows.claim: Sībawayh and al-Khalīl say an afʿal form used as an indefinite proper name does not take nunation; al-Akhfash allows it.
rows.anchor: فسيبويه والخليل لا يصرفانه، والأخفش يصرفه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Iblīs became proud after God appointed him keeper of the lowest heaven, taking the honor as a special merit.
rows.anchor: كان إبليس- لعنه الله- قد أعجب ودخله الكبر لما جعله الله خازن السماء الدنيا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second report from Ibn ʿAbbās says Iblīs’s pride arose after God sent him to defeat and kill the corrupt jinn with his army.
rows.anchor: لما بعثه الله إلى قتل الجن الذين كانوا أفسدوا في الأرض فهزمهم وقتلهم بجنده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblīs took his success as proof of superiority and, in relation to Adam, incurred unbelief and disobedience.
rows.anchor: واعتقد أن ذلك لمزية له واستحقب الكفر والمعصية في جانب آدم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: On Ibn ʿAbbās’s account, God’s “I know what you do not know” refers to the discordant pride hidden within Iblīs, unknown to the angels.
rows.anchor: وهي لا تعلم أن في نفس إبليس خلاف ذلك. قال الله لهم إني أعلم ما لا تعلمون يعني ما في نفس إبليس

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says God meant the future virtuous deeds of prophets, excellent people, and obedient descendants of Adam, which the angels did not know.
rows.anchor: يعني أفعال الفضلاء من بني آدم

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say God taught Adam the names by immediate inspiration, giving him necessary knowledge.
rows.anchor: تعليم آدم هنا عند قوم إلهام علمه ضرورة

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others say Adam was taught through speech, either by an angel or by divine speech before he descended to earth, preserving Moses’s unique distinction.
rows.anchor: بل تعليم بقول، فإما بواسطة ملك، أو بتكليم قبل هبوطه الأرض، فلا يشارك موسى- عليه السلام- في خاصته

rows.speaker: اليماني
rows.claim: The Yamānī reading has the verb in the passive, wa-ʿullima, with Ādam as its nominative subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ اليماني: «وعلم» بضم العين على بناء الفعل للمفعول

rows.speaker: أبو الفتح
rows.claim: Abū al-Fatḥ identifies this passive reading as the reading of Yazīd al-Barbarī.
rows.anchor: وهي قراءة يزيد البربري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One etymology derives Ādam from adama, reddishness tending toward black; its plurals are udm and awādim, and it is indeclinable.
rows.anchor: وآدم أفعل مشتق من الأدمة وهي حمرة تميل إلى السواد، وجمعه أدم وأوادم

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Another etymology derives Ādam from the surface of the earth, as if an angel formed it; this account gives plurals Ādamūn and awādim and requires declension.
rows.anchor: وقيل آدم وزنه فاعل مشتق من أديم الأرض، كأن الملك آدمها وجمعه آدمون وأوادم

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says Ādam is a quadriliteral verb used as a name.
rows.anchor: آدم فعل رباعي سمي به

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says Ādam was created from all the earth’s soil, so his descendants vary in color, temperament, and moral character.
rows.anchor: خلق الله آدم من أديم الأرض كلها فخرجت ذريته على نحو ذلك منهم الأبيض والأسود والأسمر

rows.speaker: جمهور الأمة
rows.claim: The majority of the community understand the names as labels for things; another group takes them to mean the persons themselves, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the first view because the verb “taught him” supports it.
rows.anchor: فقال جمهور الأمة: «علمه التسميات» وقال قوم: «عرض عليه الأشخاص»

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and Mujāhid say Adam learned the names of every created thing, small and great.
rows.anchor: علمه اسم كل شيء من جميع المخلوقات دقيقها وجليلها

rows.speaker: حميد الشامي
rows.claim: Ḥumayd al-Shāmī restricts the names to the stars.
rows.anchor: علمه أسماء النجوم فقط

rows.speaker: الربيع بن خثيم
rows.claim: Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym restricts the names to the angels.
rows.anchor: علمه أسماء الملائكة فقط

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd says Adam learned only the names of his descendants.
rows.anchor: علمه أسماء ذريته فقط

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says Adam learned the names of his descendants and the angels, preferring this because the next clause says God displayed “them” to the angels.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري: «علمه أسماء ذريته والملائكة» ، واختار هذا ورجحه بقوله تعالى: ثم عرضهم على الملائكة.

rows.speaker: النقاش عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Naqqāsh transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās that God taught Adam one word from which he recognized all names.
rows.anchor: حكى النقاش عن ابن عباس أنه تعالى علمه كلمة واحدة عرف منها جميع الأسماء

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say Adam learned generic names such as mountains, horses, and valleys, without assigning the names his descendants later used.
rows.anchor: علمه أسماء الأجناس، كالجبال والخيل والأودية ونحو ذلك، دون أن يعين ما سمته ذريته منها

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba says Adam learned the names of everything God created on earth.
rows.anchor: علمه أسماء ما خلق في الأرض

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say Adam learned names in one language, while his descendants later agreed on names for other things.
rows.anchor: علمه الأسماء بلغة واحدة، ثم وقع الاصطلاح من ذريته فيما سواها

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others say Adam learned names in every language spoken by his descendants.
rows.anchor: بل علمه الأسماء بكل لغة تكلمت بها ذريته

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Ibn Jinnī reports Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī’s extreme claim that Adam knew everything, even grammar as advanced as Sībawayh’s; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this wrong on several grounds.
rows.anchor: حكى ابن جني عن أبي علي الفارسي أنه قال: «علم الله تعالى آدم كل شيء، حتى إنه كان يحسن من النحو مثل ما أحسن سيبويه»

rows.speaker: أكثر العلماء
rows.claim: Most scholars say God taught Adam the uses of every thing and what is beneficial for it.
rows.anchor: علمه تعالى منافع كل شيء ولما يصلح

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say God displayed the objects to Adam during the teaching; others say He described them without displaying their physical forms.
rows.anchor: عرض عليه الأشخاص عند التعليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya regards both object-display and verbal-description accounts as possibilities people have held.
rows.anchor: وهذه كلها احتمالات، قال الناس بها

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb reads the feminine singular “then He displayed them.”
rows.anchor: ثم عرضها

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads the feminine plural “then He displayed them.”
rows.anchor: ثم عرضهن

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وغيره
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd and others say God displayed the objects themselves to the angels; Ibn ʿAbbās and others say He displayed the names.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن مسعود وغيره: عرض الأشخاص. وقال ابن عباس وغيره: عرض الأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the names meant all things, “displayed them” can mean presenting each community or kind; if they meant labels, Ubayy’s feminine reading fits.
rows.anchor: عرضهم أمة أمة ونوعا نوعا، ومن قال في الأسماء إنها التسميات استقام على قراءة أبي: «عرضها»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine plural “them” can refer to the objects because the word “names” can signify the objects named.
rows.anchor: إن لفظ الأسماء يدل على الأشخاص، فلذلك ساغ أن يقول للأسماء عرضهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anbiʾūnī means “inform me”; nabaʾ means news, and the word nabīʾ derives from it.
rows.anchor: وأنبئوني معناه: أخبروني، والنبأ الخبر، ومنه النبيء

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some infer that the command to inform the angels charges them with what they cannot do, showing that such a charge is permissible because God knew they lacked the knowledge.
rows.anchor: يخرج من هذا الأمر بالإنباء تكليف ما لا يطاق، ويتقرر جوازه

rows.speaker: المحققون من أهل التأويل
rows.claim: More discerning exegetes reject the impossible-charge reading: the command only elicits an acknowledgment and confirmation.
rows.anchor: ليس هذا على جهة التكليف وإنما هو على جهة التقرير والتوقيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative “these” naturally indicates that visible persons were present when God displayed them to the angels.
rows.anchor: هؤلاء ظاهره حضور أشخاص، وذلك عند العرض على الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not require “name” to mean its referent, despite Makki and al-Mahdawī’s view; the demonstrative can point to absent referents through their names or to displayed bodies.
rows.anchor: وليس في هذه الآية ما يوجب أن الاسم أريد به المسمى كما ذهب إليه مكي والمهدوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s own reading is that God taught Adam names, displayed concrete kinds first to Adam and then to the angels, and asked the angels to name them before Adam did so.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أن الله تعالى علم آدم الأسماء وعرض مع ذلك عليه الأجناس أشخاصا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hāʾulāʾ is built on kasra; shortening it is a dialect of Tamīm, some Qays, and Asad, and al-Aʿshā supplies a poetic example.
rows.anchor: وهؤلاء لفظ مبني على الكسر والقصر فيه لغة تميم وبعض قيس وأسد، قال الأعشى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites al-Aʿshā in the khafīf meter as evidence for the shortened form of hāʾulā.
rows.anchor: وهؤلاء لفظ مبني على الكسر والقصر فيه لغة تميم وبعض قيس وأسد، قال الأعشى: [الخفيف] .

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh says kuntum is jussive under the conditional, with the answer supplied by the preceding clause.
rows.anchor: وكنتم في موضع الجزم بالشرط، والجواب عند سيبويه فيما قبله

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad instead treats the answer as omitted: “if you are truthful, then inform Me.”
rows.anchor: وعند المبرد محذوف، والتقدير: إن كنتم صادقين فأنبئوني

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس وناس من أصحاب النبي
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, and some Companions take “if you are truthful” to refer to the angels’ claim that the human successor would corrupt and shed blood.
rows.anchor: معنى الآية: إن كنتم صادقين في أن الخليفة يفسد ويسفك

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others understand it as referring to the angels’ claim that, if appointed, they would glorify God and sanctify Him.
rows.anchor: صادقين في أني إن استخلفتكم سبحتم بحمدي وقدستم لي

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: A report from al-Ḥasan and Qatāda says the angels expected no creation to know more or be more honored than they; God showed Adam’s knowledge and honor to correct their assumption.
rows.anchor: روي أن الملائكة قالت حين خلق الله آدم: ليخلق ربنا ما شاء فلن يخلق خلقا أعلم منا ولا أكرم عليه

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say the angels are challenged to be truthful in their claim to knowledge; others say they must answer accurately because they know the names, a view al-Naqqāsh records.
rows.anchor: إن كنتم صادقين في جواب السؤال عالمين بالأسماء. قالوا: ولذلك لم يسغ للملائكة الاجتهاد

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqāsh argues that without the accuracy condition, the angels could have reasoned as did the man whom God caused to die for a hundred years, who guessed how long he had stayed and was not rebuked.
rows.anchor: ولو لم يشترط عليهم الصدق في الإنباء لجاز لهم الاجتهاد كما جاز للذي أماته الله مائة عام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says all these explanations of the angels’ truthfulness are possible.
rows.anchor: وهذا كله محتمل

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī rejects an interpretation reported from some exegetes that in kuntum means “when you were.”
rows.anchor: معنى إن كنتم «إذ كنتم» . قال الطبري: وهذا خطأ.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s announcement that He would place a successor on earth tests the angels, brings about their response, and instructs them through Adam’s teaching and honor.
rows.anchor: هذا منه امتحان لهم واختبار ليقع منهم ما وقع ويؤدبهم تعالى من تعليم آدم وتكريمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Subḥānaka means declaring God transcendent and affirming that no one knows anything of His knowledge except what He teaches; it is accusative as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وسبحانك معناه: تنزيها لك وتبرئة أن يعلم أحد من علمك إلا ما علمته، وسبحانك نصب على المصدر

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī parses subḥānaka as an annexed vocative rather than a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: نصبه على أنه منادى مضاف

rows.speaker: الزهراوي
rows.claim: Al-Zahrawī says mā is accusative as the object of ʿallamtanā, while another parsing makes it nominative as a substitute for the predicate of the acquittal; anta may emphasize innaka’s pronoun or begin a clause with al-ʿalīm as predicate.
rows.anchor: موضع ما من قولهم ما علمتنا نصب ب علمتنا، وخبر التبرئة في لنا،

rows.speaker: الزهراوي
rows.claim: The continuation parses al-ʿalīm as the predicate of anta and the sentence as the predicate of inna, or as a nonparsing separator.
rows.anchor: والعليم خبره، والجملة خبر «إن» ، أو فاصلة لا موضع لها من الإعراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿAlīm means “the Knowing,” with an added sense of abundance and comprehensiveness of what is known in God’s case.
rows.anchor: والعليم معناه: العالم، ويزيد عليه معنى من المبالغة والتكثير من المعلومات في حق الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥakīm means “the Ruler,” with an added sense of intensification.
rows.anchor: والحكيم معناه الحاكم، وبينهما مزية المبالغة

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others take al-Ḥakīm to mean “the One who makes things firm”; the cited verse calls al-samīʿ “the One who makes hear.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه المحكم كما قال عمرو بن معديكرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interpretation of ḥakīm as “making firm” belongs to the attributes of action.
rows.anchor: هذا من صفات الفعل

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Another group defines al-Ḥakīm as the One who prevents corruption, linking the word to the horse’s bridle and citing Jarīr’s use of aḥkimū for restraining fools.
rows.anchor: الحكيم المانع من الفساد، ومنه حكمة الفرس مانعته

rows.speaker: جرير
rows.claim: Jarīr’s line uses aḥkimū to mean restrain or control, as evidence for this sense of ḥakīm.
rows.anchor: أبني حنيفة أحكموا سفهاءكم ... إني أخاف عليكم أن أغضبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vocative yā carries an attention-getting sense.
rows.anchor: يا حرف نداء مضمن معنى التنبيه

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says the vocative’s governing verb is implicit, as though the speaker says “I want” or “I call.”
rows.anchor: والعامل في المنادى فعل مضمر كأنه يقول: أريد أو أدعو

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī says the vocative particle takes the work of an implicit verb and thereby governs; he argues it is the only particle that independently combines with nouns.
rows.anchor: العامل حرف النداء عصب به معنى الفعل المضمر فقوي فعمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel is Jacob, son of Isaac, son of Abraham; the Hebrew name means “servant of God,” since Isra means servant and El is God’s name.
rows.anchor: وإسرائيل هو يعقوب بن إسحاق بن إبراهيم عليهم السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name has several Arabic forms, including a Tamīmī form Israʾīn.
rows.anchor: وهو اسم أعجمي يقال فيه إسراءل وإسرائيل وإسرائيل، وتميم تقول إسرائين

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī offers another derivation: Isra refers to strength in captivity, as if God tightened and strengthened Jacob’s constitution.
rows.anchor: إسرا- مأخوذ من الشدة في الأسر كأنه الذي شد الله أسره

rows.speaker: نافع والحسن والزهري وابن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ, al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī, and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read Israʾīl without the hamza in Isra.
rows.anchor: وروي عن نافع والحسن والزهري وابن أبي إسحاق ترك همز إسراييل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr here means recollection in the heart, the opposite of forgetting.
rows.anchor: وهذا منها ذكر القلب الذي هو ضد النسيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Niʿma is grammatically singular but collective in meaning; its final yā is vowelled before the article, though it may be quiescent and elided, and the vowel is preferable because it preserves a written letter.
rows.anchor: والنعمة هنا اسم الجنس فهي مفردة بمعنى الجمع، وتحركت الياء من نعمتي لأنها لقيت الألف واللام

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī gives examples of Israel’s favor: prophets from among them, manna and quails, rescue from Pharaoh’s torture, and water gushing from the rock.
rows.anchor: بعثة الرسل منهم وإنزال المن والسلوى، وإنقاذهم من تعذيب آل فرعون، وتفجير الحجر

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another explanation identifies the favor as granting them the lifetime of Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: النعمة هنا أن دركهم مدة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others identify the favor as granting Israel knowledge of the Torah and making them its people and bearers.
rows.anchor: هي أن منحهم علم التوراة وجعلهم أهله وحملته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats the specific favors as examples and prefers the general meaning of the word.
rows.anchor: وهذه أقوال على جهة المثال، والعموم في اللفظة هو الحسن

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makkī says the address targets only Israelites who believed in Muḥammad, since an unbeliever cannot receive God’s favor.
rows.anchor: أن المخاطب من بني إسرائيل بهذا الخطاب هم المؤمنون بمحمد صلى الله عليه وسلم، لأن الكافر لا نعمة لله عليه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وجمهور العلماء
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and most scholars say the address includes all Israelites living in the Prophet’s time, believers and unbelievers; “you” refers to their ancestors by an Arabic usage that addresses descendants for ancestral acts.
rows.anchor: بل الخطاب لجميع بني إسرائيل في مدة النبي عليه السلام، مؤمنهم وكافرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the address is restricted to believers in Muḥammad, “you” is direct and the commands that follow call for continued commitment.
rows.anchor: استقام الضمير في عليكم ويجيء كل ما توالى من الأوامر على جهة الاستدامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Fulfill My covenant and I will fulfill yours” is a command followed by its response.
rows.anchor: وأوفوا بعهدي أوف بعهدكم أمر وجوابه

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says the command’s response is jussive because the command carries a conditional sense; fulfilling a covenant means committing to the stipulated act.
rows.anchor: جزم الجواب في الأمر من معنى الشرط، والوفاء بالعهد هو التزام ما تضمن من فعل

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī reads awfi with an open wāw and doubled fāʾ, conveying intensification.
rows.anchor: قرأ الزهري: «أوف» بفتح الواو وشد الفاء للتكثير

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority take God’s covenant broadly as all His commands, prohibitions, and instructions, including the Torah’s mention of Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: ذلك عام في جميع أوامره ونواهيه ووصاياه فيدخل في ذلك ذكر محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم في التوراة

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Another view identifies the covenant with God’s command to take what He gave them firmly.
rows.anchor: العهد قوله تعالى: خذوا ما آتيناكم بقوة

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj identifies the covenant as God’s pledge to the Children of Israel; their covenant is His promise to admit them to Paradise, and their fulfillment signifies His fulfillment rather than causing it, since a cause cannot precede its effect.
rows.anchor: العهد قوله تعالى: ولقد أخذ الله ميثاق بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “Me alone fear,” iyyāya is a noun followed by the first-person pronoun, or the whole form is itself the noun; it is accusative after an implied verb delayed for emphasis.
rows.anchor: الاسم ايا والياء ضمير ككاف المخاطب، وقيل إياي بجملته هو الاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A preceding verb would require a light attached pronoun, so the implied verb is delayed; the yā after nūn is dropped at the verse ending.
rows.anchor: وامتنع أن يتقدر مقدما لأن الفعل إذا تقدم لم يحسن أن يتصل به إلا ضمير خفيف

rows.speaker: ابن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Abī Isḥāq reads the final yā in fārhabūnī.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي إسحاق بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āminū means “believe”; muṣaddiqan is an accusative circumstantial expression linked either to the pronoun in anzaltu or to mā; “what I sent down” is the Qurʾān and “what is with you” the Torah.
rows.anchor: وآمنوا معناه صدقوا، ومصدقا نصب على الحال من الضمير في أنزلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ban on being the first disbeliever grammatically warns the first group but also includes everyone who follows; the first bears a share of the burden of those who imitate it.
rows.anchor: الأول والثاني وغيرهما داخل في النهي، ولكن حذروا البدار إلى الكفر به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awal is the predicate of kāna; Sībawayh says it has no corresponding verb because its first two radicals are defective, while others derive it from waʾala, “escape.”
rows.anchor: ونصب أول على خبر كان. قال سيبويه: أول أفعل لا فعل له لاعتلال فائه وعينه

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Other grammarians derive awal from āla, with hamza transposition, easing, substitution, and assimilation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه من آل فهو أأول قلب فجاء وزنه أعفل، وسهل وأبدل وأدغم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kāfir is singular in form although it refers to a group, since an afʿal form can take a singular inflected noun and convey a collective.
rows.anchor: ووحد كافر وهو بنية الجمع لأن أفعل إذا أضيف إلى اسم متصرف من فعل جاز إفراد ذلك الاسم

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poetic line illustrates the singular form used for a group with the collective sense of “worst of those who hunger.”
rows.anchor: وإذا هم طعموا فألأم طاعم ... وإذا هم جاعوا فشر جياع

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh understands awal as an indefinite shortened form of the definite phrase “the first disbeliever”; another view means the first group to disbelieve.
rows.anchor: سيبويه يرى أنها نكرة مختصرة من معرفة كأنه قال ولا تكونوا أول كافرين به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Quraysh disbelieved before, “first disbeliever” here means first among the People of the Book, who were viewed as knowledgeable authorities.
rows.anchor: وقد كان كفر قبلهم كفار قريش، فإنما معناه من أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some take the pronoun in “in it” to refer to Muḥammad; others refer it to the Torah because “what is with you” implies it; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the latter makes the literal firstness coherent.
rows.anchor: فقيل على محمد عليه السلام، وقيل على التوراة إذ تضمنها قوله: لما معكم

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Another view makes the pronoun refer to the Qurʾān, implied by “what I sent down.”
rows.anchor: وقيل الضمير في به عائد على القرآن، إذ تضمنه قوله بما أنزلت

rows.speaker: طائفة
rows.claim: One group says Jewish scholars were forbidden to teach their religion for wages; their own books say to teach freely as they had been taught freely.
rows.anchor: إن الأحبار كانوا يعلمون دينهم بالأجرة، فنهوا عن ذلك وفي كتبهم: علم مجانا كما علمت مجانا

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others say the scholars received regular food or stipends in return for their teaching and were forbidden to accept it.
rows.anchor: كانت للأحبار مأكلة يأكلونها على العلم كالراتب فنهوا عن ذلك

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others say the scholars took bribes to alter the Torah’s account of Muḥammad; Ibn ʿAṭiyya links this explanation to the parallel in al-Māʾida.
rows.anchor: إن الأحبار أخذوا رشى على تغيير قصة محمد عليه السلام في التوراة

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Another interpretation is a warning against trading God’s commands, prohibitions, and signs for the brief and worthless life of this world.
rows.anchor: ولا تشتروا بأوامري ونواهي وآياتي ثمنا قليلا، يعني الدنيا ومدتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear of God includes a threat, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya distinguishes the stronger warning implicit in “fear Me” from “be mindful of Me.”
rows.anchor: وبين «اتقون» و «ارهبون» فرق، ان الرهبة مقرون بها وعيد بالغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Labas al-amr means to mix or confuse a matter by blending it with what resembles it, as in mixing truth with falsehood.
rows.anchor: يقال «لبست الأمر» بفتح الباء ألبسه، إذا خلطته ومزجت بينه بمشكله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited line about one troop “wearing” another could mean mixing troops or literally clothing them.
rows.anchor: وكتيبة لبستها بكتيبة فالظاهر أنه من هذا المعنى، ويحتمل أن يكون المعنى من اللباس

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya says the Jews affirmed that Muḥammad was a prophet but claimed he was sent to others: their affirmation was true, their denial of his mission to them false.
rows.anchor: قالت اليهود: محمد نبي مبعوث، لكن إلى غيرنا، فإقرارهم ببعثه حق وجحدهم أنه بعث إليهم باطل

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says Jewish hypocrites outwardly professed faith, which was true, while inwardly concealing unbelief, which was false.
rows.anchor: كان من اليهود منافقون فما أظهروا من الإيمان حق، وما أبطنوا من الكفر باطل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid interprets the command as forbidding the blending of Judaism and Christianity with Islam.
rows.anchor: معناه لا تخلطوا اليهودية والنصرانية بالإسلام

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd takes the truth as the Torah and the falsehood as their alteration of its mention of Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: المراد ب الحق التوراة، و «الباطل» ما بدلوا فيها من ذكر محمد عليه السلام،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Talbisū is jussive under the prohibition; taktumū may be coordinated in the jussive or made accusative by an implied an and coordinated with an implied verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وتلبسوا جزم بالنهي، وتكتموا عطف عليه في موضع جزم، ويجوز أن يكون في موضع نصب بإضمار «أن»

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: The Kufan grammarians parse taktumū as accusative through waw al-ṣarf.
rows.anchor: تكتموا نصب بواو الصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here “the truth” specifically means the matter of Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: والحق يعني به أمر محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause “while you know” can be circumstantial; alternatively it is a specific testimony that they knew the truth about Muḥammad, not general knowledge, and so is not circumstantial.
rows.anchor: ولم يشهد لهم تعالى بعلم وإنما نهاهم عن كتمان ما علموا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These expressions show that knowingly committing the sin aggravates it and makes the person more disobedient than an ignorant offender.
rows.anchor: دليل على تغليظ الذنب على من واقعه على علم، وأنه أعصى من الجاهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Establish prayer means display its form and maintain it with its conditions, like raising someone from sitting to standing; a poem uses the same verb for horses forming a line for battle.
rows.anchor: أظهروا هيئتها وأديموها بشروطها، وذلك تشبيه بإقامة القاعد إلى حال ظهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The zakāt commanded here is obligatory, as shown by the community’s consensus that it must be performed.
rows.anchor: والزكاة في هذه الآية هي المفروضة بقرينة إجماع الأمة على وجوب الأمر بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakāt may derive from growth: giving reduces wealth immediately but increases it through blessing or divine reward.
rows.anchor: وسمي الإخراج من المال زكاة وهو نقص منه من حيث ينمو بالبركة أو بالأجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another derivation is purification: payment purifies wealth from the liability owed to the poor, and the Prophet calls what is taken for zakāt people’s “dirt.”
rows.anchor: وقيل الزكاة مأخوذة من التطهير، كما يقال زكا فلان أي طهر

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In the Muwaṭṭaʾ, the Prophet calls the zakāt payment “people’s dirt.”
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم سمى في الموطأ ما يخرج في الزكاة أوساخ الناس

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some take the mention of bowing as a part standing for the whole prayer, since bowing is one of its pillars.
rows.anchor: جعل الركوع لما كان من أركان الصلاة عبارة عن الصلاة كلها

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others say bowing is specified because Israelites did not include it in their prayer.
rows.anchor: إنما خص الركوع بالذكر لأن بني إسرائيل لم يكن في صلاتهم ركوع

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: A group says “with those who bow” adds attendance at communal prayer, which the initial prayer command did not require.
rows.anchor: فأمرهم بقوله مع بشهود الجماعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rukūʿ literally means bending the body; Labīd uses it in a description of bending while standing.
rows.anchor: والركوع في اللغة الانحناء بالشخص

rows.speaker: لبيد
rows.claim: Labīd’s line uses rākiʿ for a person bending as he stands.
rows.anchor: أدب كأني كلما قمت راكع

rows.speaker: الأضبط بن قريع
rows.claim: Al-Aḍbaṭ ibn Qurayʿ uses rukūʿ metaphorically for falling in rank after a person’s fortunes rise.
rows.anchor: لا تعاد الضعيف علك أن تر ... كع يوما والدهر قد رفعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do you command people” is a rhetorical question meant as rebuke; birr gathers forms of good and obedience, each of which can itself be called birr.
rows.anchor: خرج مخرج الاستفهام، ومعناه التوبيخ، و «البر» يجمع وجوه الخير والطاعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tansawna means “you leave” or “neglect,” as in the parallel wording in al-Tawba.
rows.anchor: وتنسون بمعنى تتركون كما قال الله تعالى: نسوا الله فنسيهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the Jewish scholars urged their followers to follow the Torah while they themselves violated it by denying its description of Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: كان الأحبار يأمرون أتباعهم ومقلديهم باتباع التوراة، وكانوا هم يخالفونها في جحدهم منها صفة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم
